metadata.title: Why Your Embeddings Lie About Similarity
metadata.description: An AI/STEM explainer: vector embeddings power search and RAG, but 'close in vector space' is not the same as 'actually relevant.' Cosine similarity can rank a wrong-but-similarly-worded chunk above the right answer. The teach is that similarity is a measurement, not a truth.

beats.narration_text: Hello Amruta. Every AI search system rests on one quiet assumption: that things close together in vector space are things that actually belong together. Most of the time that's true. But 'similar' and 'relevant' are not the same word — and when they split apart, your search returns confident garbage. Today: why embeddings lie about similarity.

props.topic: WHY YOUR EMBEDDINGS LIE ABOUT SIMILARITY
props.runningText: similarity is a measurement, not a truth
output: Embeddings turn text into points in space
'Close together' is assumed to mean 'related'
But similar-sounding ≠ relevant
When they split, search returns confident garbage

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one breath. An embedding turns a sentence into a list of numbers — a point in a huge invisible space. Search works by finding the nearest points. But 'nearest' is measured by wording and surface pattern, not by meaning or truth. So a chunk that merely sounds like your question can beat the chunk that actually answers it.

output: Text → a point in high-dimensional space
Search = find the nearest points
'Nearest' rewards surface similarity
Sounds-like can beat actually-answers

beats.narration_text: Picture two sentences. 'The cat sat on the mat.' And 'The mat sat on the cat.' To you, those mean opposite things. To an embedding built on word overlap, they're almost identical — same words, same neighborhood, nearly the same point. The model measured the vocabulary, not the logic. That gap is where the lie lives.

props.topic: THE GAP · SAME WORDS, OPPOSITE MEANING
props.command: # 'cat sat on mat' vs 'mat sat on cat'
props.runningText: same words → nearly the same vector → opposite meaning
output: Two sentences, opposite meaning
Same vocabulary → nearly the same point
The embedding measured words, not logic
Cosine similarity says: 'basically the same'

beats.narration_text: So why does this happen? Cosine similarity — the math most systems use — measures the angle between two vectors. A small angle means 'similar direction.' But direction is built from which words appear and how often, not from what the sentence asserts. Negation, word order, who-did-what-to-whom — the things that carry meaning — barely move the angle.

props.title: cosine similarity — what it actually measures
props.code:
# similarity = cos(angle between the two vectors)
#   small angle  -> 'very similar'
#   large angle  -> 'unrelated'
#
# but the vector's direction is built from:
#   which words appear, and how often
#
# it is NOT built from:
#   negation ('not'), word order, who did what to whom
#
# result: 'X approves Y' and 'X rejects Y' can sit
#         almost on top of each other. same words,
#         opposite claim, tiny angle.

beats.narration_text: In a RAG system this is quietly dangerous. You ask a question, the retriever grabs the top-similar chunks, and the language model dutifully answers from them — trusting they're relevant. If a similar-but-wrong chunk ranked first, the model builds a fluent, confident answer on a false foundation. Nothing errors. Nothing warns you. The similarity score looked great.

props.command: # retriever grabs top-similar → model trusts it
props.runningText: high similarity score, wrong chunk, confident answer
output: You ask; retriever grabs top-similar chunks
The model trusts they're relevant
A similar-but-wrong chunk poisons the answer
No error, no warning — the score looked great

beats.narration_text: So what's the honest takeaway? Similarity is a measurement, not a verdict. 'Close in vector space' is a useful signal, but it is not proof of relevance. Treat the top result as a candidate to check, not an answer to trust. The number is telling you 'this looks alike' — never 'this is right.'

props.artifactTitle: Why Your Embeddings Lie About Similarity
props.artifactHeading: Similarity is a measurement, not a truth
artifactLines: Embeddings measure surface pattern, not meaning or truth.
Cosine similarity rewards shared words — not correct claims.
Negation and word order barely move the score.
Treat the top hit as a candidate to verify, never a proven answer.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take any embedding search you rely on. Feed it a question, then look at the second and third results — not just the first. Ask: is this one actually relevant, or does it just share words with my query? You'll start seeing the lie. And once you see it, you'll never fully trust a raw similarity score again.

props.runningText: relevant, or just sharing words with the query?
output: 1. Run a query through your embedding search
2. Look at results 2 and 3, not just the top
3. Ask: relevant, or just similar wording?
4. Once you see the lie, you can't unsee it

beats.narration_text: Similarity is not truth. It's a hint that needs checking. Next time: why turning up the temperature often turns up the wrong answers. Hello Amruta, signing off.
